lead: Consensus is the problem of making a group of processes agree on one value even when some processes crash or lie. Each process starts with a proposed value. Every correct process must eventually decide the same value, and that value must come from one of the proposals. Replicated databases, leader election in cloud systems, and payment ledgers all need this agreement. The number of failures a system can survive depends on two choices: the failure type (crash or Byzantine) and the timing model (synchronous or asynchronous).
prereq: You need Unit 4 on synchronous versus asynchronous systems and message ordering, and the group communication ideas in Chapter 5.6.

sections.h3: The agreement problem and its conditions

blocks.text: A distributed system has N processes. A process is correct if it follows its algorithm and does not fail during the run. A faulty process may stop (crash failure) or behave arbitrarily, including sending false values (Byzantine failure). Consensus starts when each process proposes a value. A decision is final: once a process decides, it does not change its mind. The chapter uses value 1 for attack and 0 for retreat in the general example.

items: Termination: every correct process eventually decides a value.
Agreement: no two correct processes decide different values.
Validity (also called integrity): the decided value was proposed by some process.

blocks.text: Timing matters. In a synchronous model every message has a known bounded delay and every process runs at a known bounded speed. In an asynchronous model no bound on message delay or process speed is known. These models decide which algorithms are possible. A crash failure is easier than a Byzantine failure, and a synchronous system is easier than an asynchronous one.

sections.h3: Crash failures: majority voting in f+1 rounds

blocks.text: Let f be the maximum number of processes that may crash. The system can tolerate f crashes when N ≥ 2f+1, so a strict majority of processes are correct. For example, with f = 1, N = 3 is enough; two correct processes outvote one silent process.

blocks.where: N is the total number of processes; f is the maximum number of crash failures; a majority is more than N/2 processes.

items: Each process starts with its own proposed value.
For f+1 rounds, every process sends the set of values it knows to every other process.
After each round, a process keeps the value that appears in a majority of the values it has received.
After f+1 rounds, every correct process decides that majority value.

blocks.text: Why f+1 rounds? A value needs to survive f silent processes. After f+1 exchanges, every correct process has heard the same majority of values. If fewer than f+1 rounds are used, a crashed process can hide a value from some correct process and break agreement. See Chapter 5.6 for process groups and retries.

A Byzantine process can send different values to different peers, stay silent, or lie about what it received. Let f now be the maximum number of Byzantine processes, including a faulty commander. The oral-messages algorithm needs N ≥ 3f+1, that is f ≤ (N−1)/3. With f = 1, at least four generals are needed. Three is not enough because one traitor can split the two loyal lieutenants.

blocks.where: N is total processes; f is maximum Byzantine faults; for f = 1, N must be at least 4.

items: The commander sends its value to every lieutenant.
Each lieutenant forwards the value it received to every other lieutenant.
Each loyal lieutenant takes a majority over the value from the commander and the values forwarded by the other lieutenants.
The algorithm uses f+1 rounds; each round lowers the number of traitors by one.

blocks.text: The figure shows f = 1 with four generals. L3 is the traitor. It tells L1 and L2 that the commander said 0. L1 still receives 1 from C, 1 from L2, and 0 from L3, so its majority is 1. L2 receives 1 from C, 1 from L1, and 0 from L3, so its majority is also 1. Agreement holds because two loyal values outvote one lie. With N = 3 and f = 1 the same vote has only two values, 1 and 0, and no majority.

The FLP result (Fischer, Lynch, Paterson) says no deterministic algorithm can solve consensus in a purely asynchronous system if even one process may crash. The algorithm can be safe, but it cannot guarantee termination in every run. Practical systems therefore use synchrony, randomisation, or failure detectors to make progress.

items: Paxos: proposers send values to acceptors; a value is chosen when a majority of acceptors accept the same proposal. It keeps safety under crashes and asynchronous delays, but may stall.
Raft: a leader is elected by a majority, and it replicates a log to followers. It is designed to be easier to understand than Paxos.
Two-phase commit (2PC): a coordinator asks all participants to prepare, then sends commit or abort. It can block if the coordinator crashes after some participants prepare.
Three-phase commit (3PC): adds a pre-commit phase to reduce blocking, but it still needs timing assumptions to be safe.
Failure detector: a local module that suspects which processes have crashed; an eventually perfect detector is enough for some consensus algorithms.

blocks.text: Use the right model before choosing a protocol. Synchronous crash-tolerant systems can use majority voting. Asynchronous systems need Paxos, Raft, or a randomised algorithm. Byzantine systems need 3f+1 replicas, as used in some blockchains and safety-critical control.

figure.caption: Two rounds with four generals: the traitor L3 sends a false 0, but L1 and L2 each collect 1, 1, 0 and decide 1.

spec.aria: Two rounds of the Byzantine generals algorithm with four processes: the traitor L3 sends a false value 0, but the two loyal lieutenants still collect a majority of 1 and agree on attack.

examples.question: Four generals are C, L1, L2, L3. The maximum number of Byzantine generals is f = 1, and L3 is the traitor. C orders attack, value 1. L3 tells L1 and L2 that C said 0. Run the oral-messages algorithm for f = 1. State N, the minimum N required by 3f+1, the number of values each loyal lieutenant collects, the majority threshold, and the decision of L1 and L2.
steps: N = 4 and f = 1. The minimum is 3f+1 = 3(1)+1 = 4, so N = 4 is exactly enough.
Round 1: C sends 1 to L1, L2 and L3. L3 is faulty; it will lie in round 2.
Round 2: L1 forwards 'C said 1' to L2 and L3. L2 forwards 'C said 1' to L1 and L3. L3 forwards 'C said 0' to L1 and L2.
L1 collects: from C 1, from L2 1, from L3 0. That is 3 values. Majority threshold = floor(3/2)+1 = 2. Count of 1 is 2, count of 0 is 1, so L1 decides 1.
L2 collects: from C 1, from L1 1, from L3 0. Same counts. L2 decides 1.
Agreement holds: both loyal lieutenants decide 1, which was C's proposed value. With N = 3, each loyal lieutenant would collect only 2 values, 1 and 0, and no strict majority would exist.
examples.answer: N = 4, f = 1, minimum N = 3f+1 = 4, each loyal lieutenant collects 3 values, majority threshold 2, and both L1 and L2 decide 1 (attack).
examples.check:
N = 4
f = 1
min_n = 3 * f + 1
collected = N - 1
threshold = collected // 2 + 1
votes = [1, 1, 0]
d1 = 1 if votes.count(1) >= threshold else 0
d2 = 1 if votes.count(1) >= threshold else 0
print(N)
print(f)
print(min_n)
print(collected)
print(threshold)
print(d1)
print(d2)

traps: Using N ≥ 2f+1 for Byzantine faults. That bound is only for crash faults; Byzantine faults need N ≥ 3f+1, that is f ≤ (N−1)/3.
Thinking FLP forbids every consensus algorithm. FLP applies only to deterministic asynchronous systems with even one crash failure; synchronous and randomised systems can still always agree.
Swapping validity and agreement. Validity says the decided value was proposed; agreement says no two correct processes decide differently.
Counting the Byzantine commander as extra. The value f includes every faulty process, commander or lieutenant.
Forgetting that f+1 rounds are message exchanges, not seconds. The round count is a correctness requirement.

quiz.q: State the three conditions of consensus.
quiz.a: Termination: every correct process eventually decides. Agreement: no two correct processes decide different values. Validity (integrity): the decided value was proposed by some process.

quiz.q: Why does a Byzantine fault need N ≥ 3f+1 while a crash fault needs only N ≥ 2f+1?
quiz.a: A crash fault is silent, so a majority of correct processes can outvote it. A Byzantine process can lie differently to different peers, so the correct processes must be enough to form two overlapping majorities and still outnumber the liars. That requires at least 3f+1 processes.

quiz.q: A system may have up to 2 Byzantine faulty processes. What is the minimum total number of processes needed?
quiz.a: Use N ≥ 3f+1 with f = 2. N ≥ 3(2)+1 = 7. Minimum N = 7.

quiz.q: A crash-tolerant system has N = 9 processes. What is the maximum number of crash failures it can tolerate under majority voting?
quiz.a: Use N ≥ 2f+1. 9 ≥ 2f+1, so 8 ≥ 2f, f ≤ 4. Maximum f = 4.

quiz.q: Does Paxos violate the FLP result because it is used in asynchronous networks? Explain.
quiz.a: No. FLP says a deterministic asynchronous algorithm cannot guarantee termination with one crash. Paxos keeps safety, but it may stall without synchrony or randomisation. It does not guarantee progress in every asynchronous run.

quiz.q: In the four-general example, why does N = 3 with f = 1 fail even if the commander is loyal?
quiz.a: With N = 3 there are C and two lieutenants. If one lieutenant is a traitor, a loyal lieutenant collects only two values: the commander's 1 and the traitor's 0. There is no strict majority, so agreement cannot be guaranteed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real systems build consensus into replicated logs: etcd and Consul use Raft, while many databases use Paxos-style quorums. Blockchains mix Byzantine fault tolerance with economic incentives. Search for the Raft paper, Paxos Made Simple, the FLP impossibility result, and Byzantine fault-tolerant state machine replication. Compare crash-tolerant and Byzantine protocols before reading industrial case studies.
